Power and Sample Size for an Intraclass Correlation Test

Source: R/power_icc.R
power_icc.Rd

Computes the power of the F test of an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) used by icc_test(), or solves for the number of subjects, the number of measurements per subject, the ICC under the alternative, or the significance level that gives a target power. Exactly one of n, k, rho1, power and sig.level must be NULL; that one is computed from the others, as in stats::power.t.test().

Usage

power_icc(
  n = NULL,
  k = 2,
  rho0 = 0,
  rho1 = NULL,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = NULL,
  model = c("oneway", "twoway"),
  unit = c("single", "average"),
  missing = 0,
  alternative = c("two.sided", "greater", "less"),
  method = c("exact", "approximate")
)

Arguments

n

Number of subjects.

k

Number of measurements (items: trials, raters or occasions) per subject. When solved for, the smallest whole number of at least 2 that reaches the target is returned.

rho0

The ICC under the null hypothesis (default 0).

rho1

The ICC under the alternative hypothesis.

sig.level

Significance level (Type I error rate; default 0.05).

power

Power of the test (1 minus the Type II error rate).

model

"oneway" (default) or "twoway". "twoway" means the consistency ICC, ICC(C,1) of icc_test(); the absolute agreement ICC is not supported (see Details).

unit

"single" (default) for the reliability of a single measurement, or "average" for the reliability of the mean of the k measurements (ICC(k) or ICC(C,k)), as in icc_test(). With "average", the ICC values are on the average-measure scale and k cannot be solved for. See Details.

missing

The expected proportion of measurements (subject-by-item cells) that will be missing, analysed with icc_test(method = "reml"). The default, 0, gives the exact complete-data calculation; values above 0 give an approximation (see Details). For subjects who will be lost entirely, reduce n instead.

alternative

"two.sided" (default), "greater", or "less", as in icc_test(). A design planned with the defaults matches the analysis run with the defaults.

method

"exact" (default) computes power from the exact distribution of the F statistic. "approximate" uses the closed form of Walter, Eliasziw and Donner (1998), available only for model = "oneway".

Value

An object of class "power.htest", printed by stats::print.power.htest(), with elements n, k, rho0, rho1, sig.level, power, alternative, method and note.

Details

Exact power. For the one-way and the two-way consistency ICC with complete data, the F ratio of the subject mean square to the error mean square is a scaled central F variable whatever the true ICC \(\rho\): $$F \sim \frac{1 + (k-1)\rho}{1 - \rho} F_{n-1, \nu_2},$$ with \(\nu_2 = n(k-1)\) (one-way) or \((n-1)(k-1)\) (two-way). The test of \(H_0: \rho = \rho_0\) (McGraw & Wong, 1996) divides the F ratio by the same factor at \(\rho_0\), so its power is a single F probability (Donner & Eliasziw, 1987). Non-integer n is allowed, as in stats::power.t.test(); round up to the next whole number of subjects.

Approximate power uses the closed form of Walter, Eliasziw and Donner (1998), $$n = 1 + \frac{2k (z_{1-\alpha} + z_{1-\beta})^2}{(k-1)(\log C_0)^2}, \quad C_0 = \frac{1 + k\theta_0}{1 + k\theta_1}, \quad \theta = \frac{\rho}{1 - \rho},$$ with \(\alpha/2\) in place of \(\alpha\) for a two-sided test. Walter et al. (and the PASS software) write n for the number of measurements per subject and k for the number of subjects; here n is always the number of subjects and k the number of measurements per subject. The exact method is preferred; the approximation is provided to reproduce published tables.

Two-sided tests. When solving for rho1 with alternative = "two.sided", the solution above rho0 is returned; use alternative = "less" (with the significance level halved) for the one below.

Average-measure ICCs. The average-measure ICC is the Spearman-Brown projection of the single-measure ICC to k measurements, \(k\rho / (1 + (k-1)\rho)\), so a test about ICC(k) or ICC(C,k) is the same F test as the test about the corresponding single-measure ICC, and its interval is the projection of the single-measure interval. With unit = "average" the calculations are therefore exact, not approximations; k must be given because it defines the quantity being planned for.

Missing measurements (approximate). With missing = p > 0, the calculation uses the observed-data quantities that icc_test(method = "reml") uses for incomplete data: \(N = nk(1 - p)\) observations, \(\bar{k} = N/n\) measurements per subject in the scale factor of the F ratio and in the interval, and error degrees of freedom \(N - n - k + 1\) (two-way) or \(N - n\) (one-way). This is an approximation: the F distribution is exact only for complete data. In simulations of the REML analysis (one-way and two-way ICCs, 15 or 40 subjects, 3 or 5 items, 15% or 30% of measurements missing completely at random or 30% at random depending on the first measurement; 1000 replicates per setting), the approximate power was within 0.035 of the simulated power (Monte Carlo SE 0.016) and the approximate median interval width within 2.2% of the simulated median. The REML test itself was slightly liberal with 30% missing (type I error up to 0.069 missing completely at random and 0.073 at random, for a nominal 0.05), which the simulated power includes. A warning is given above 30% missing. The calculation assumes each subject keeps at least one measurement.

Planning other designs. These functions are exact only for the one-way and two-way consistency ICCs with complete, normally distributed data. They can still guide the planning of other ICC studies, as long as the direction of the error is kept in mind:

  • Absolute agreement ICC (ICC(A,1), and the CCC for two methods). Not supported exactly: its test has no exact F distribution, and because its denominator degrees of freedom depend on the sample, its power "cannot be determined exactly" (McGraw & Wong, 1996, footnote 3). When the items (trials, raters, methods) differ little systematically, ICC(A,1) is close to ICC(C,1) and the consistency calculation is a good guide. When they differ, the agreement test and interval also depend on the item mean square, which has only k - 1 degrees of freedom: power is lower and intervals wider than the consistency calculation says, most of all with 2 or 3 items. Treat the consistency result as a lower bound on the number of subjects; simulation would be needed for a precise answer.

  • Missing measurements. Use missing for measurements missing here and there (see below). For subjects who will be lost entirely, plan for the subjects who complete the study and recruit \(n / (1 - d)\) for an expected dropout d.

  • Non-normal data. The exact calculations assume normality. With skewed or heavy-tailed data the F-based intervals are wider and cover less than planned (see icc_test() and reli_err_test() for simulations), so allow a margin or plan for the bootstrap with a larger sample.

References

Donner, A., & Eliasziw, M. (1987). Sample size requirements for reliability studies. Statistics in Medicine, 6(4), 441-448. doi:10.1002/sim.4780060404

McGraw, K. O., & Wong, S. P. (1996). Forming inferences about some intraclass correlation coefficients. Psychological Methods, 1(1), 30-46. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.1.1.30

Walter, S. D., Eliasziw, M., & Donner, A. (1998). Sample size and optimal designs for reliability studies. Statistics in Medicine, 17(1), 101-110. doi:10.1002/(SICI)1097-0258(19980115)17:1<101::AID-SIM727>3.0.CO;2-E

See also

precision_icc() for the sample size for a confidence interval of a given width; icc_test() for the analysis.

Examples

# Subjects needed to show an ICC above 0.6 when it is 0.8, with 2 trials
power_icc(rho0 = 0.6, rho1 = 0.8, k = 2, power = 0.8,
          alternative = "greater")
#> 
#>      Power calculation for the one-way ICC, ICC(1) (exact F distribution) 
#> 
#>               n = 38.90078
#>               k = 2
#>            rho0 = 0.6
#>            rho1 = 0.8
#>       sig.level = 0.05
#>           power = 0.8
#>     alternative = greater
#> 
#> NOTE: n is the number of subjects; round up to a whole number.
#>       n = number of subjects, k = measurements per subject
#> 

# Power with 30 subjects and 3 trials
power_icc(n = 30, k = 3, rho0 = 0.5, rho1 = 0.75, alternative = "greater",
          model = "twoway")
#> 
#>      Power calculation for the two-way consistency ICC, ICC(C,1) (exact F distribution) 
#> 
#>               n = 30
#>               k = 3
#>            rho0 = 0.5
#>            rho1 = 0.75
#>       sig.level = 0.05
#>           power = 0.8835267
#>     alternative = greater
#> 
#> NOTE: n = number of subjects, k = measurements per subject
#> 

# Trials needed with 20 subjects
power_icc(n = 20, k = NULL, rho0 = 0.5, rho1 = 0.8, power = 0.9,
          alternative = "greater")
#> 
#>      Power calculation for the one-way ICC, ICC(1) (exact F distribution) 
#> 
#>               n = 20
#>               k = 3
#>            rho0 = 0.5
#>            rho1 = 0.8
#>       sig.level = 0.05
#>           power = 0.9
#>     alternative = greater
#> 
#> NOTE: n = number of subjects, k = measurements per subject
#>
